account: A 34-year-old man with no medical history consulted his primary care physician. His smartwatch had detected “heart arrhythmias” while he was asymptomatic. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial contractions (PACs). A cardiologist found a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35% with a dilated ventricle. Despite guideline-directed heart-failure therapy, he returned months later with palpitations and chest pain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed an LVEF of 15%. Computed tomography angiography excluded coronary disease. Holter recordings showed a PAC burden of 30–50%. High-density three-dimensional mapping located the ectopic focus at the left inferior pulmonary vein. Radiofrequency ablation terminated the arrhythmia. At six months he was symptom-free, with an LVEF of 50% and fewer than 1% PACs. Spironolactone was stopped. Soubh, Rasenack, Haarmann, Zabel and Bergau published the case report in European Heart Journal - Case Reports on 15 April 2025. The authors are at the Department of Cardiology and Pneumology, University Medical Center Göttingen, Germany. They call it the first reported PAC-related arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy initially detected by a wearable. The report gives no event dates. The journal received the case report on 5 October 2024, so the six-month follow-up and every event before it took place by that day. The report states neither the brand nor the model of the watch, nor the form of its alert. On 19 December 2025, cardiologists in Thessaloniki published a review that cites the case. They note that premature atrial contractions are a major source of false-positive atrial fibrillation alerts on smartwatches.

fields.headline: A smartwatch alert leads a 34-year-old to treatment for a weakened heart
fields.title: Smartwatch “heart arrhythmias” alert leads to a diagnosis of cardiomyopathy caused by premature atrial contractions in a 34-year-old man; ablation lifts his ejection fraction from 15% to 50%

provenance.basis: SHA-256 of the public case, its assessments, and its displayed answers and notes, excluding its own identifier and the derived coverage summary.

fields.account: A 34-year-old man with no medical history consulted his primary care physician. His smartwatch had detected “heart arrhythmias” while he was asymptomatic. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial contractions (PACs). A cardiologist found a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 35% with a dilated ventricle. Despite guideline-directed heart-failure therapy, he returned months later with palpitations and chest pain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed an LVEF of 15%. Computed tomography angiography excluded coronary disease. Holter recordings showed a PAC burden of 30–50%. High-density three-dimensional mapping located the ectopic focus at the left inferior pulmonary vein. Radiofrequency ablation terminated the arrhythmia. At six months he was symptom-free, with an LVEF of 50% and fewer than 1% PACs. Spironolactone was stopped. Soubh, Rasenack, Haarmann, Zabel and Bergau published the case report in European Heart Journal - Case Reports on 15 April 2025. The authors are at the Department of Cardiology and Pneumology, University Medical Center Göttingen, Germany. They call it the first reported PAC-related arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy initially detected by a wearable. The report gives no event dates. The journal received the case report on 5 October 2024, so the six-month follow-up and every event before it took place by that day. The report states neither the brand nor the model of the watch, nor the form of its alert. On 19 December 2025, cardiologists in Thessaloniki published a review that cites the case. They note that premature atrial contractions are a major source of false-positive atrial fibrillation alerts on smartwatches.

must_hold: The PAC burden is high enough to be caught by the watch and to cause the cardiomyopathy. The authors note case reports typically exceed 30%.
The ventricular dysfunction is still reversible when the arrhythmia is eliminated
produced_by: An asymptomatic wearer whose smartwatch flagged arrhythmias and who took the flag to a physician
A primary care ECG followed by cardiology work-up including echocardiography, MRI and Holter monitoring
An electrophysiology service able to map and ablate a high-burden PAC focus

purpose: Smartwatch arrhythmia alerts are built to prompt medical review of irregular rhythms. The alert here served that purpose. The authors say that wearables are not usually credited with finding the condition that it uncovered, cardiomyopathy induced by premature atrial contractions.

ratings.reason: The alert started a series of tests in which physicians diagnosed a cardiomyopathy. The condition progressed until the left ventricular ejection fraction was 15%. Ablation restored it to 50%, and his symptoms resolved. The authors present early detection as what allowed the heart failure to be treated before further progression.
